name: Mewing

card.summary: Resting the whole tongue against the palate to reshape the face; popular online, but no research shows it changes adult jaw structure.
card.aka: orthotropics, tongue posture, oral posture training
card.note: The American Association of Orthodontists says there is no evidence it reshapes the jaw; its originator's son was struck off the UK dental register in 2024.

quick.overview:
Mewing is a do-it-yourself habit of keeping the tongue flat against the roof of the mouth, lips closed and teeth lightly together, with nasal breathing. It is named after the British orthodontist John Mew and his son Mike Mew, who promoted a wider approach called orthotropics. It spread widely on social media from 2019 and became one of the best-known practices in looksmaxxing communities.

Proponents say sustained tongue posture can push the upper jaw forward and sharpen the jawline, with the strongest effects claimed in children. Orthodontic bodies say no credible research shows it reshapes the face. The one controlled study usually cited is a small twin study of orthotropic versus conventional braces treatment, which tested professional orthotropic appliances rather than tongue posture alone.
quick.mechanism: The theory holds that the tongue's resting pressure on the palate guides upper-jaw growth forward and outward, and that jaw shape depends heavily on posture and breathing habits rather than genetics alone. Mainstream orthodontics attributes facial form mainly to genetics and growth. Some community members also say the posture temporarily lifts the hyoid bone and tightens the area under the chin, which can change how the jawline looks.
quick.risks: Gentle tongue posture is not documented to carry serious risks, though some online posts report masseter enlargement or a worse appearance from forceful versions. The main documented harms concern Mike Mew's clinical practice, which a UK regulatory tribunal examined, rather than the home technique. Orthodontic organizations warn that it may delay evidence-based treatment for real bite or jaw problems.

lead: Mewing is a self-directed practice in which a person rests the whole tongue against the roof of the mouth, keeps the lips sealed and the teeth lightly together, and breathes through the nose, with the stated aim of improving jaw and facial structure [2][3][4]. People who practise it do so to work toward a more defined jawline, a more forward upper jaw, better-looking facial profile and a stronger-looking neck-and-chin line, and many pair it with chewing, posture work and, for some, orthodontic palate expansion [6][15][17].

The term comes from John Mew (1928-2025), a British orthodontist, and his son Mike Mew, who promoted a system called orthotropics. Orthotropics holds that the resting posture of the tongue, lips and jaws during childhood guides how the face grows, and that crooked teeth and recessed jaws are largely postural rather than genetic [3][4]. John Mew traced the idea to a 1958 proposal he called the Tropic Premise [3]. Mainstream orthodontic organisations take a different view of facial growth, and Wikipedia describes mewing as an unproven technique [4].

Interest in mewing rose sharply from January 2019, driven by YouTube, then TikTok and looksmaxxing forums, and it became one of the most recognisable practices in appearance culture [4][19]. The American Association of Orthodontists (AAO) acknowledges that tongue posture plays a role in facial development, while stating that no current research shows the technique benefits the jawline [1][22]. A 2019 commentary in the Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery examined it as a possible alternative to orthognathic surgery [5]. The practice is also the subject of a long regulatory history involving both Mews, covered below [3][19][21].

paras: The technique is usually described as pressing the full length of the tongue, including the back third, flat against the palate, with the lips closed, the teeth lightly touching or close together without clenching, and attention to nasal breathing and neck posture [2][4]. Proponents describe it as a resting posture held throughout the day rather than a timed exercise. John Mew summarised the posture in the phrase "stand up straight and shut your mouth" [3].

Online communities distinguish ordinary mewing from 'hard mewing', in which people press the tongue upward with more force, and from combinations with other practices such as chewing hard foods, chin tucks and mouth taping [6]. Some forum users pair it with palate expansion by an orthodontist, treating mewing as a maintenance habit around a clinical expander [15]. Proponents also describe the posture as improving nasal breathing and the look of the neck and chin line, claims discussed in the culture section below [10].

Orthotropics claims that the face grows in the direction it is 'guided' to, and that the resting position of the tongue, lips and jaws during development steers the upper jaw forward and outward rather than downward and back. Mainstream orthodontics mainly attributes crooked teeth and jaw form to genetics and growth, and the two views have long been in open disagreement [3].

Clinically, orthotropics has used appliances as well as posture. The Biobloc system combined a palate-expanding appliance with a postural appliance. Other elements include dietary change and training a specific tongue position [3]. John Mew met the German orthodontist Rolf Fränkel in East Germany in 1968, and his account of breathing and facial growth drew on Konstantin Buteyko's work [3]. In a 2022-era YouTube context reported by trade press, Mike Mew also claimed that creating enough tongue space can influence facial growth, including 'expansion of the brain' [19].

John Roland Chandley Mew was born on 7 September 1928 in Royal Tunbridge Wells, began dental training at University College London in 1948 and qualified in 1953, later gaining a specialty in orthognathic surgery at Queen Victoria Hospital, East Grinstead, in 1956 [3]. In 1958 he proposed the Tropic Premise, which treats malocclusion as a postural problem that early intervention can prevent [3]. He practised for about three decades and helped found the International Association of Facial Growth Guidance in Fort Worth, Texas, in 1987 [3].

He also raced cars in the 1950s and 1960s and built a moated castle in Sussex in the 1990s, details that recur in media portraits of the family [3]. Grokipedia traces related ideas to early twentieth-century myofunctional therapy and the London School of Facial Orthotropics, founded in 1983 [2].

Mew's views drew opposition from mainstream British orthodontists. In the 1980s he was fined by the NHS for inappropriate treatment; he appealed to the High Court in 1987, where the judge called the criticisms wholly unwarranted and ruled in his favour [3]. The General Dental Council (GDC) reprimanded him in 2010 over advertisements containing misleading claims, including claims denigrating orthodontics; he did not dispute the charge and described himself as a whistleblower. The GDC revoked his registration in 2017 over false advertising and breach of patient confidentiality [3]. He died on 25 June 2025 aged 96 [3].

Mike Mew promoted tongue posture to a wide online audience, and the term 'mewing' came into use in online communities during the 2010s [2]. Google search interest began rising in January 2019; The Guardian covered mewing as a YouTube face-shaping craze in March 2019, and in 2020 the New York Times Magazine profiled the Mews and their links to incel communities [4]. Influencers posting how-to videos drew hundreds of millions of views, according to Discover magazine, and TikTok searches reportedly passed 4.7 billion [22][19]. Mike Mew appeared on the British television programme This Morning, per Wikipedia's account of John Mew [3].

The practice spread particularly within looksmaxxing and incel subcultures, and by 2023 it had become a general internet meme, associated with 'brain rot' humour and with the character of the Rizzler [4]. The British Orthodontic Society expelled Mike Mew around 2018 to 2019 for continuing to promote orthotropic positions, and he launched a petition against the decision [4][3].

On 6 November 2024 the GDC's Professional Conduct Committee, sitting through the Dental Professionals Hearings Service, found Mike Mew's fitness to practise impaired by misconduct and erased him from the Dentists' Register [21][19]. The charges concerned orthotropic treatment of two child patients between 2013 and 2019 and claims made to parents and in a 2017 YouTube video. The GDC said his approaches were not sufficiently supported by scientific evidence and liable to cause harm, and that he made misleading statements about the need for treatment [21][19]. One patient, a boy aged six in 2018, was reported to have had prolonged seizure-like episodes after extended use of head and neck gear [19].

Mew compared the GDC's position to the Church's case against Galileo and said the regulator was more concerned with protecting the orthodontic industry than children [19]. He appealed to the High Court. In a judgment dated 15 May 2026, the court dismissed his grounds relating to expert evidence and the committee's findings, described the committee's conclusions as unassailable, and noted that orthotropics itself was not on trial, the charges being about his conduct toward two patients. The judgment records that he accepted orthotropics lacks a substantial evidence base [21].
No controlled trial has tested tongue posture alone, as practised in mewing, for changing facial structure.

A small controlled study of 12 identical twins compared fixed orthodontic appliances with orthotropic (growth guidance) treatment without fixed appliances, assessed ten years later by 12 lay judges. Most conventionally treated twins were judged less attractive after treatment, while most orthotropically treated twins were judged improved, and the traditionally treated cases relapsed more often [7]. The study examined professionally delivered orthotropic treatment, not self-directed mewing.

A 2019 commentary in the Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery examined mewing as an alternative to orthognathic surgery [5], and a 2026 article in the Journal of Clinical Orthodontics discussed the mewing trend [8]. A 1992 paper by an orthodontic author put forward hypotheses that tongue and lip posture influence oropharyngeal development and Eustachian tube function, proposing that early orthotropic treatment might direct growth forward; it reports clinical impressions rather than a controlled trial [9].

The AAO states that tongue posture plays a role in facial development but that changing tongue position alone does not correct misaligned teeth, reshape the jaw or remove the need for orthodontic treatment. Its explainer, published in March 2025, says there is no current research showing the technique benefits the jawline or oral health [1]. AAO president Myron Guymon told Discover magazine that proper tongue posture plays a role in oral health, while mewing 'oversimplifies the complexities of facial structure' [22].

The AAO lists possible downsides of excessive or uneven tongue pressure, including tooth shifting, crowding or gaps, TMJ pain and speech difficulties, and notes that any resulting problems could make later braces more complex [1]. It advises that attempts to move teeth or align jaws be supervised by an orthodontist [1]. Wikipedia reports that most orthodontists do not regard mewing as a viable alternative to jaw surgery [4]. Proponents counter that orthotropics rests on a different view of growth in which posture and breathing shape the face, and that mainstream orthodontics focuses too narrowly on teeth [2]. Discover also cites a 2020 BioScience study reporting jawlines shrinking over recent decades, with researchers suggesting harder chewing as one compensation [22].

Mewing is among the most discussed practices on looksmax.org, with threads from users reporting results, others describing none, and others suggesting it matters mainly in early adolescence [10][11]. Thread titles range from claims that it works with how-to guides to claims that it ruined a face, and others discuss whether it works only in childhood or only under certain conditions [12][13][14][23][24]. A 2025 qualitative study of an online looksmaxxing community analysed 8,072 comments and noted that the community encourages substantial body modification such as mewing and leg lengthening, and argued that participation harms users' health [14].

The word has also become general slang. Some people say 'mewing' in jest or describe a 'mewing face', and students reportedly mew in class to avoid answering questions [4]. Related accessories and terms appear in community threads, such as a 'mewing ring' [25].

Orthodontic palate expansion, which widens the upper jaw with a fixed or removable appliance, is a clinical procedure used to treat narrow palates and some bite problems [18]. Forum users often compare it with mewing, and some report pursuing both [15]. Chewing, chin tucks, mouth taping and myofunctional therapy are other posture and muscle practices frequently listed alongside mewing [6].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, mewing is treated as a baseline practice that members debate constantly, with advice about age cut-offs, hard mewing, and how it combines with chewing or palate expansion [10][15].

claims.claim: Mewing can bring the maxilla forward and sharpen the jawline
claims.believers: Proponents say consistent tongue posture guides forward growth, and members post progress pictures and accounts of patients of John Mew [16][17].
claims.experts: The AAO says there is no current research showing a jawline benefit, and no controlled trial has tested tongue posture alone [1][7].

claims.claim: Mewing mostly works in childhood and does little after puberty
claims.believers: A thread on maxilla mewing says results at ages 14 to 17 are small, with disagreement over whether to expect 0, 1-2 or more millimetres [10].
claims.experts: Orthodontic sources generally say skeletal change from appliances is more achievable during growth, but no published study measures this for tongue posture alone [18][4].

claims.claim: Mewing temporarily lifts the hyoid and makes the jawline look sharper
claims.believers: A forum poster says the posture lifts the hyoid bone and gives a sharper-looking jaw, even if bone does not change [10].
claims.experts: No published studies have examined this effect.

claims.claim: Mewing can harm the face or teeth
claims.believers: Some users post that mewing worsened their appearance, as in a thread titled for that claim [12].
claims.experts: The AAO says excessive or uneven tongue pressure may shift teeth, contribute to bite or TMJ problems and cause speech difficulty, though it cites no trial [1].

claims.claim: Mewing reduces anxiety and improves breathing
claims.believers: A forum thread claims scientific proof that mewing lowers anxiety [20].
claims.experts: No published studies were found examining mewing and anxiety.

claims.claim: Orthotropics is held back by the orthodontic establishment
claims.believers: Mike Mew compared the GDC's position to the case against Galileo and said the regulator was protecting the orthodontic industry; a forum thread title claims orthodontists are 'evil' [19][15].
claims.experts: The High Court judgment records that orthotropics was not itself on trial and that Mew accepted it lacks a substantial evidence base; experts at the hearing found no objective evidence supporting his treatment claims [21].

claims.claim: Tongue space can influence brain expansion
claims.believers: Mike Mew said in a YouTube video that creating enough tongue space can influence facial growth and cause expansion of the brain [19].
claims.experts: No published studies were found testing this claim; the GDC found some of his statements misleading [21].

angle.text: People mew in the hope of a sharper jawline, a more forward midface and a better facial profile, using a free habit that takes no equipment. Proponents say the strongest effect is during growth, and some say posture alone can make the jaw and neck look more defined. Orthodontic bodies say tongue posture alone has not been shown to reshape the jaw.
